etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Shift from Old Japanese 七日 (nanuka), attested in the Man'yōshū of circa 759 CE; ultimately from Proto-Japonic *nanuka.
The nanoka reading is first cited to a text from the late Edo period.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 伯母(おば) (oba) + さん (san).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
The 連用形 (ren'yōkei, “continuative or stem form”) of verb 余る (amaru, “to be left over, to be in excess”). Appears in the Kojiki of 712 CE.
Also encountered with geminate reading あんまり (anmari) as an emphatic form for the adjective and adverb uses. This form appears in the 1400s.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨pi₁karu⟩ → */pʲikaru/ → /ɸikaru/ → /hikaru/
From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *pikaru.
The initial hika- is related to ぴかぴか (pikapika, “glitteringly, sparklingly”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Ultimately from Middle Chinese 醫學 (MC 'i haewk). First attested in Japanese in the late 1400s in the 文明本節用集 (Bunmei Hon Setsuyō-shū, “Bunmei Edition Dictionary”), published some time during the Bunmei era (8 June 1469 through 9 August 1487).
By surface analysis, 医(い) (i) + 学(がく) (-gaku).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 午(ご) (go, “noon”) + 後(ご) (go, “after-, post-”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Originally from regular classical adjective 厳し (kibishi, “tight, close, without gaps”), first cited to roughly 830.
This earlier form later shifted conjugation patterns, from the so-called "-ku adjective" to the "-shiku adjective" pattern. The two conjugation types appear to have been in broadly free variation, with both forms developing the strict; severe senses in parallel. Historically, while there was some overlap, there does appear to be a sense distinction in Classical Japanese texts, wherein the older "-ku adjective" form was used more commonly to express the more objective qualities of "tight, close", while the "-shiku adjective" was used more commonly to express the more subjective qualities of "severe; harsh".
The "-shiku adjective" pattern is first cited from the late 900s.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Early Middle Japanese adjective 厳(いつく)し (itsukushi), with the 終(しゅう)止(し)形(けい) (shūshikei, “predicative form”) ending in し (shi) first replaced with the 連(れん)体(たい)形(けい) (rentaikei, “attributive form”) ending in しき (shiki), and then with the medial /-k-/ falling out to result in an ending of しい (shii).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 喫茶(きっさ) (kissa, “drinking tea”) + 店(てん) (-ten, “shop; store”)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Cognate with Okinawan 食(か)むん (kamun, “to eat”). Doublet of 醸む (kamu, “to brew”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
⟨ko₂we⟩ → */kəwe/ → /kowe/ → /koe/
From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *kəwai.
Further derivation unknown.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Middle Chinese 聲 (MC syeng).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/sjau/ → /ɕau/ → /ɕɔː/ → /ɕoː/
From Middle Chinese 聲 (MC syeng).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 大 (tai, “of great intensity”) + 切 (setsu, “urgent, pressing, close”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
*/tipisasi/ → /tiɸisasi/ → /t͡ɕiwisaɕi/ → /t͡ɕiːsaɕi/ → /t͡ɕiːsai/
Ultimate derivation uncertain.
The initial chi element appears in other words with similar meanings of small, such as ちょっと (chotto, “a little bit”, adverb), from ちっと (chitto), emphatic geminate derived from even earlier ちと (chito), in which と (to) marks an adverb.
Possibly related to ちび (chibi, “small and round”, often with overtones of cuteness), itself apparently derived from 粒(つぶ) (tsubu, “small round thing”, such as a grain of rice).
First attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720, albeit in the ideographic spelling 細. First attested unambiguously in the late 800s, early 900s in the attributive inflection with the phonetic spelling 知比佐伊 (tifisai).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese かへる (kape₁ru), from Proto-Japonic *kaperu.
Cognate with 返(かえ)る (kaeru, “to return”), by extension of returning to one's home.
Compare 帰(かえ)す (kaesu, “to send someone home”, transitive).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/otopito/ → /otoɸito/ → /otowito/ → /*otowuto/ → /otouto/ → /otoːto/
Originally a compound of 弟 (oto, “younger sibling”) + 人 (hito, “person”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *mat-. Cognate with Okinawan 待ちゅん (machun, “to wait (for)”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Semantic shift from Classical Japanese 強(こは)し (kofashi, “stiff, strong, tough”), modern 強(こわ)い (kowai). A folk etymology from the Ehon Hyaku Monogatari derives it from 狐(こ)者(わ)異(い) (kowai, literally “ghost of a glutton”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *to. According to Beckwith (2004), related to the sole certainly attested Kara word 梁 (/⁠dol, dor(?)⁠/, “gate, door”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Sino-Japanese, from Middle Chinese 戶 (MC huX).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
First attested in Japanese in 1563 with a sense of "technique; method or means by which something is handled or processed".
Later repurposed as a calque of English mechanical art by Nishi Amane in the encyclopedia Hyakugaku Renkan.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese 來 (ku), from Proto-Japonic *ku. Compare the development of modern する (suru) from Old Japanese す.
First attested in the Kojiki of 712.
Cognate with Kunigami 来ん (sun), Miyako 来 (ksï), Okinawan 来ーん (chuun), Yaeyama 来ん (kïn), Yonaguni 来ん (kun).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From 来(き) (ki, continuative form of etymology 1) + 至(いた)る (itaru).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 毎 (mai-, “every”) + 年 (toshi, “year”)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 毎 (mai-, “every”) + 年 (nen, “year”)

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese. First attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE. From Proto-Japonic *ikay.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
/tʲie/ → /ti/ → /t͡ɕi/
From Middle Chinese 池 (MC drje).
Used in Old Japanese as 借音 (shakuon) kana for ⟨ti⟩ in the Nihon Shoki (720 CE).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From the classical lower bigrade verb(ヤ行下二段活用) 消ゆ.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Early Middle Japanese adjective 深(ふか)し (fukashi), with the 終(しゅう)止(し)形(けい) (shūshikei, “predicative form”) ending in し (shi) first replaced with the 連(れん)体(たい)形(けい) (rentaikei, “attributive form”) ending in き (ki), and then with the medial /-k-/ falling out to result in an ending of い (i). From Old Japanese. First attested in the Kojiki of 712 CE. From Proto-Japonic *puka.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: The fukai changes to bukai as an instance of rendaku (連濁).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: From Old Japanese. Appears in the Kojiki of 712 CE, and in the Man'yōshū completed some time after 759 CE. From Proto-Japonic *yak-.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Orthographic borrowing from Chinese 砂糖 (shātáng).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
From Old Japanese. Compound of 目(ま) (ma, “eye”, ancient combining form of modern 目(め) (me)) + 門(と) (to, “gate, opening”), in reference to an opening for looking through.
Alternatively, may be a compound of 間(ま) (ma, “gap”) + 門(と) (to, “gate, opening”).
First cited in some references to a text from 794, and also found in the Man'yōshū of 759.
The Microsoft Windows sense is a semantic loan from English Windows.

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Compound of 美(び)術(じゅつ) (bijutsu, “art”) + 館(かん) (kan, “public building”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text:
Originally a compound of 去に (ini, “going away”, the 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of the verb 去(い)ぬ (inu, “to go away”)) + し (shi, “wind; (by extension) direction”, as seen in other ancient-derived words as 嵐 (arashi, “storm”, literally “wild + wind”), 旋風 (tsumuji, “whirlwind”), 東 (higashi, “east”, from older pi muka si, literally “sun + facing + wind/direction”)).
First cited in the Kojiki of 712, with the phonetic spelling 爾斯 (nisi).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Possibly a corruption of Mandarin 西 (xī, “west”).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Inherited from Old Japanese. The noun sense is a nominalization of the 連(れん)用(よう)形(けい) (ren'yōkei, “stem or continuative form”) of classical adjective 近(ちか)し (chikashi, “near”), equivalent to modern 近(ちか)い (chikai).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: Related to 憤(むずか)る (muzukaru) and 憤(むつか)る (mutsukaru).

etymologies.heading: Etymology
etymologies.text: 食料(しょくりょう) (shokuryō) + 品(ひん) (-hin)
